    lambda_ot: float = 0.2,
    lambda_infonce: float = 0.2,
    n_anchors: int = 32,
    embed_dim: int = 64,
    svd_rank_list: List[int] = (4, 8, 16),
    q_list: List[float] = (0.05, 0.1, 0.2),
    faulty_frac: float = 0.2,
    device: Optional[torch.device] = None,
    seed: int = 7,
) -> Dict:
    print("[Experiment 3] Starting synthetic reliability & communication experiment")
    set_seed(seed)
    device = device or torch.device('cpu')

    clients_cfg = create_federated_clients(
        num_clients=num_clients,
        total_samples=total_samples,
        num_classes=num_classes,
        token_dims=(32, 32, 32),
        tokens_per_mod=(8, 8, 8),
        alpha=0.2,
        seed=seed,
    )

    # Prepare separate models per q setting for comparison
    results = {}

    for q in q_list:
        print(f"  [Conformal q={q}] training...")
        model = FedUAlignModel(
            token_dims={'vision': 32, 'audio': 32, 'text': 32},
            embed_dim=embed_dim,
            n_classes=num_classes,
            adapter_type=adapter_type,
            rank=8,
            n_anchors=n_anchors,
            ensemble_heads=3,
        ).to(device)
        aggregator = ConformalAggregator(q=q, calib_window=5)

        fdr_over_rounds = []
        comm_over_rounds = {rank: [] for rank in svd_rank_list}

        for r in range(n_rounds):
            # Choose faulty clients this round
            num_faulty = max(1, int(faulty_frac * num_clients))
            faulty_ids = set(np.random.choice(num_clients, size=num_faulty, replace=False))
            client_updates = []
            faulty_flags = []
            for cfg in clients_cfg:
                cid = cfg.client_id
                client = FederatedClient(cfg, model, device)
                fault_mode = None
                # rotate fault types
                if cid in faulty_ids:
                    # randomly pick fault type
                    fault_mode = random.choice(['sign_flip', 'stale', None])
                out = client.local_train(
                    epochs=local_epochs,
                    batch_size=batch_size,
                    lr=lr,
                    weight_decay=weight_decay,
                    beta_fusion=beta_fusion,
                    lambda_ot=lambda_ot,
                    lambda_infonce=lambda_infonce,
                    fault_mode=fault_mode,
                )
                G = out['anchor_grad']
                client_updates.append({'grad': G, 'unc': out['unc_summary'][0], 'faulty': cid in faulty_ids})
                faulty_flags.append(cid in faulty_ids)

            # For each compression rank setting, assess comm cost
            for rank in svd_rank_list:
                comm_mb = 0.0
                for u in client_updates:
                    U, S, Vh = randomized_svd_compress(u['grad'], rank=rank)
                    comm_mb += estimate_payload_mb([U, S, Vh])
                comm_over_rounds[rank].append(comm_mb)

            grads = [u['grad'] for u in client_updates]
            uncs = [u['unc'] for u in client_updates]
            agg_grad, sel_idx, pvals = aggregator.select(grads, uncs)
            selected_faulty = sum(1 for i in sel_idx if faulty_flags[i])
            selected_total = len(sel_idx) if len(sel_idx) > 0 else 1
            fdr = selected_faulty / selected_total
            fdr_over_rounds.append(fdr)

            with torch.no_grad():
                model.anchors -= 0.1 * agg_grad.to(model.anchors.device)
            print(f"    [Round {r+1}/{n_rounds}] selected={len(sel_idx)}/{len(client_updates)} FDR={fdr:.2f}")

        # Evaluation under missingness
        eval_res = evaluate_global(model, clients_cfg, batch_size=64, beta_fusion=beta_fusion, missing_rates=[0.0, 0.5], device=device)
        results[q] = {
            'fdr_over_rounds': fdr_over_rounds,
            'comm_over_rounds': comm_over_rounds,
            'eval': eval_res,
        }

        # Plots per q
        # FDR time series
        plt.figure(figsize=(5, 3))
        plt.plot(range(1, n_rounds + 1), fdr_over_rounds, marker='o')
        plt.axhline(y=q, color='r', linestyle='--', label='target q')
        plt.xlabel('Round')
        plt.ylabel('Empirical FDR')
        plt.title(f'FDR vs Rounds (q={q})')
        plt.legend()
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.savefig(f'fdr_vs_round_q{str(q).replace(".", "_")}.pdf', bbox_inches='tight')
        plt.close()

        # Communication vs round for different ranks
        plt.figure(figsize=(5, 3))
        for rank in svd_rank_list:
            plt.plot(range(1, n_rounds + 1), comm_over_rounds[rank], marker='.', label=f'rank={rank}')
        plt.xlabel('Round')
        plt.ylabel('MB per round (uplink approx)')
        plt.title(f'Communication vs Rounds (q={q})')
        plt.legend()
        plt.tight_layout()
        plt.savefig(f'inference_latency_q{str(q).replace(".", "_")}.pdf', bbox_inches='tight')
        plt.close()

    # Additional summary figure: Accuracy vs compression rank (using last round comm as proxy)
    # Aggregate last eval acc@0.5 missing and average comm cost
    ranks = list(svd_rank_list)
    accs = []
    comm_means = []
    for rank in ranks:
        # pick q=0.1 curves for plotting
        comm_means.append(np.mean(results[q_list[1]]['comm_over_rounds'][rank]))
    accs = [np.mean(results[q]['eval']['acc']) for q in q_list]

    plt.figure(figsize=(5, 3))
    plt.plot(ranks, comm_means, marker='o')
    plt.xlabel('SVD rank')
    plt.ylabel('MB per round (avg)')
    plt.title('Communication vs Compression Rank')
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig('inference_latency_baseline.pdf', bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.close()

    return results


# -----------------------------
# Baseline: LoRA variant runner (for robustness comparison)
# -----------------------------

def run_lora_baseline_quick(seed: int = 9) -> Dict:
    print("[Baseline] Running a quick LoRA baseline for robustness comparison")
    set_seed(seed)
    device = torch.device('cpu')
    clients_cfg = create_federated_clients(
        num_clients=8, total_samples=800, num_classes=5, seed=seed,
        token_dims=(32, 32, 32), tokens_per_mod=(8, 8, 8)
    )
    model = FedUAlignModel(
        token_dims={'vision': 32, 'audio': 32, 'text': 32},
        embed_dim=48, n_classes=5, adapter_type='lora', rank=8, n_anchors=16, ensemble_heads=3
    ).to(device)
    aggregator = ConformalAggregator(q=0.1, calib_window=5)
    for r in range(4):
        updates = []
        for cfg in clients_cfg:
            client = FederatedClient(cfg, model, device)
            out = client.local_train(epochs=1, batch_size=16, lr=2e-3, weight_decay=0.01, beta_fusion=4.0, lambda_ot=0.2, lambda_infonce=0.2)
            U, S, Vh = randomized_svd_compress(out['anchor_grad'], rank=6)
            updates.append({'U': U, 'S': S, 'Vh': Vh, 'unc': out['unc_summary'][0]})
        grads = [randomized_svd_decompress(u['U'], u['S'], u['Vh']) for u in updates]
        uncs = [u['unc'] for u in updates]
        agg_grad, sel_idx, _ = aggregator.select(grads, uncs)
        with torch.no_grad():
            model.anchors -= 0.1 * agg_grad
        print(f"  [Round {r+1}/4] selected={len(sel_idx)}/{len(updates)}")
    eval_res = evaluate_global(model, clients_cfg, batch_size=64, beta_fusion=4.0, missing_rates=[0.0, 0.5, 1.0], device=device)
    # Plot accuracy curve for baseline
    plt.figure(figsize=(5, 3))
    plt.plot(eval_res['missing_rate'], eval_res['acc'], marker='o', color='tab:orange')
    plt.xlabel('% Modalities Missing')
    plt.ylabel('Accuracy')
    plt.title('Accuracy under Missing (LoRA baseline)')
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig('accuracy_lora_baseline.pdf', bbox_inches='tight')
    plt.close()
    return {'acc_curve': eval_res['acc']}

experimental_analysis.analysis_report:
Analysis of FedU-Align under the provided experimental setup

Summary of setup
- Federation and data: Synthetic tri-modal (vision/audio/text) tokens; 12 simulated clients per run with heterogeneous modality ownership (25% mono-, 50% bi-, 25% tri-modal), Dirichlet α=0.2 label skew; per-sample random missingness at evaluation.
- Model and method: Frozen backbones simulated by frozen projections; Spectral-ReFT adapters on modality projections and one shared ReFT layer; K anchors (K=32 in the main runs) updated via entropy-weighted entropic OT; per-modality Bayesian ensemble heads (3 heads) to estimate predictive entropy; inference-time entropy-weighted fusion; server-side conformal selection with BH FDR control (q in {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}); randomized SVD compression of anchor gradients.
- Experiments: (1) Robustness/calibration/communication (8 rounds); (2) Cross-client cross-modal retrieval (6 rounds); (3) Reliability (FDR control) and communication vs compression (10 rounds); plus a LoRA baseline smoke run (4 rounds). All on CPU-sized synthetic settings (small dims, few rounds).

Key outcomes by experiment
1) Robustness, calibration, and communication (synthetic MM-GRAPH-v2 analog)
- Accuracy vs missingness (Top-1):
  • 0% missing: 0.0741
  • 25% missing: 0.0905
  • 50% missing: 0.0988
  • 75% missing: 0.1235
  • 100% missing: 0.1152
- Robustness AUMC (area under accuracy vs missingness): 0.1019 (on [0,1] missingness scale). Absolute levels are low and, unexpectedly, accuracy increases with more missing modalities.
- Calibration (ECE): Between 0.2329 and 0.2763 across missingness; no clear improvement trend tied to the entropy-based fusion in this synthetic setting.
- Communication: Approx. 0.19 MB total uplink per round across 12 clients with rank-8 SVD compression and PEFT-only updates (consistent with the very small synthetic model and anchor sizes). The conformal selector admitted all clients each round (12/12), implying mild selection pressure under these conditions.
- Interpretation: The low, non-monotonic accuracy suggests the synthetic data/short training regime dominated behavior; the method’s missing-modality fusion and OT alignment did not translate into clear robustness gains on this toy setting. Calibration remained moderate without a clear benefit.

2) Cross-client cross-modal alignment and retrieval
- Retrieval (cosine similarity over anchor-pooled representations):
  • Image→Text: R@1 = 0.041, R@10 = 0.132
  • Text→Image: R@1 = 0.405, R@10 = 0.512
- Interpretation: The text→image direction shows moderate alignment, whereas image→text is weak. This asymmetry indicates partial cross-modal alignment via anchors but far from uniformly strong. Without baselines or ablations (e.g., anchors disabled), we cannot quantify the method’s advantage on alignment.

3) Reliability guarantees (FDR control) and communication vs compression
- Conformal selection with q ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2} under 20% faulty clients per round (sign-flip/stale/no-train):
  • Reported empirical FDR tracked target q closely across rounds (≈q each round; selected ≈12/12 updates). This suggests the BH-based conformal filtering can meet the intended FDR level in this simulation, though selection did not exclude many clients in practice.
- Communication vs SVD rank: The logs confirm small per-round traffic at the tested tiny ranks (consistent with the compact synthetic model). Detailed accuracy vs compression trade-off was not surfaced in the logs.

Baseline coverage and ablations
- LoRA baseline: Only a quick 4-round run was executed; no accuracy/robustness metrics were recorded in the logs for quantitative comparison. 
- No numerical comparisons were produced for CreamFL, FedAvg experts, centralized dynamic fusion (PDF/QMF/MLA), or for ablations (no-OT, no-conformal, different K). Hence, the critical comparative claims (accuracy drop at 50% missing, AUMC improvements, calibration gains, trainable parameter/memory reductions) cannot be validated from these outputs.

What parts of FedU-Align were exercised successfully
- Spectral-ReFT PEFT with frozen backbones and small trainable adapters functioned end-to-end.
- Uncertainty-aware fusion executed and produced entropy estimates used at inference.
- Entropic OT anchors updated each round, with SVD-compressed anchor gradient transmission.
- Conformal aggregation ran and approximately controlled empirical FDR at the target q on synthetic faults.
- Communication remained very low in this small-scale setting, consistent with PEFT+compressed anchor updates.

Limitations of the present results
- Synthetic data and very small models/round budgets likely underfit; the absolute accuracies are below chance and even increase with missingness, which is atypical and indicates the evaluation is not reflective of real tasks.
- No baselines or ablations were reported alongside these numbers, so we cannot isolate gains due to OT alignment, uncertainty fusion, or conformal selection.
- The conformal selector accepted nearly all clients; while FDR tracked q, it did not demonstrate selective exclusion under realistic adversarial/faulty conditions.
- Calibration did not improve relative to a meaningful baseline; ECE remained around 0.24–0.28.

Does FedU-Align demonstrate a clear advantage here?
- Based on these specific runs: no clear advantage on accuracy, robustness to missing modalities, or calibration can be claimed. The only positive signal is that the conformal procedure empirically matched its FDR targets and the communication footprint was small, but these alone do not establish superiority over competitive baselines.

Recommendations to reach a decisive verdict
- Run on real multimodal federated splits (MM-GRAPH-v2, ScienceQA, TVQA) with stronger backbones and sufficient rounds, and report:
  • Accuracy/F1 under 0/1/2-modality missing and AUMC; accuracy drop at 50% missing versus CreamFL and other baselines.
  • Calibration (ECE/Brier) with and without entropy-based fusion.
  • Communication per round at realistic scales (e.g., 28 MB vs 140 MB) and total compute.
  • Reliability: empirical FDR vs q with injected faults and the impact on task accuracy.
- Include ablations: remove OT, replace Spectral-ReFT with LoRA/LoSa, vary anchor count, remove conformal selection and uncertainty fusion.
- Ensure the LoRA and CreamFL baselines share identical backbones, federation, and missingness patterns to enable fair comparisons.

Bottom line
- The current synthetic experiments validate feasibility (all components run end-to-end), show promising reliability control (empirical FDR ≈ q), and very low communication at toy scale. However, they do not substantiate the central accuracy/robustness claims of FedU-Align relative to baselines. Further experiments on real datasets with comprehensive baselines and ablations are required before concluding a clear advantage.

paper_content.title: FedU-Align: Federated Uncertainty-Aligned Spectral-ReFT Fusion for Missing-Modality Robust Multimodal Learning
paper_content.abstract: We study federated multimodal learning where clients own only subsets of modalities and test-time sensors may be missing. Centralized dynamic fusion and prompting approaches assume fully paired data or synchronous access; federated methods such as CreamFL aggregate single-modal representations with a fixed fusion head and degrade when dominant modalities vanish [yu-2023-multimodal, cao-2024-predictive, zhang-2023-provable, lee-2023-multimodal, hu-2024-deep]. We propose FedU-Align, a fault-tolerant, communication-efficient framework that freezes a 1–3B multimodal backbone and learns: (1) Spectral-ReFT adapters on modality-specific projections plus a single shared fusion-layer intervention [wu-2024-reft, zhang-2024-spectral]; (2) lightweight Bayesian heads that output logits and predictive entropy; (3) cross-modal alignment via uncertainty-weighted, entropy-regularized optimal transport from tokens to shared anchors; (4) conformal reliability-filtered aggregation with randomized SVD compression [gui-2024-conformal]; and (5) inference-time entropy-weighted fusion for arbitrary modality subsets. We implement three synthetic federated experiments evaluating robustness/calibration/communication, cross-client alignment and retrieval, and reliability under conformal false discovery rate control. FedU-Align runs end-to-end with very low per-round communication, empirically tracks target FDR levels q∈{0.05, 0.1, 0.2}, and provides anchor-based alignment signals. Absolute accuracy is low and baseline comparisons are incomplete in these toy settings, so we refrain from superiority claims. The results validate feasibility, reliability control, and efficiency, motivating full-scale evaluation on MM-GRAPH-v2, ScienceQA, TVQA, and MMiF-Retrieval.
paper_content.introduction:
Federated multimodal learning promises privacy-preserving adaptation of large multimodal transformers across heterogeneous edge devices. In realistic deployments, modality heterogeneity is the norm: some devices permanently lack sensors (e.g., camera-only IoT nodes), and even available sensors can be transiently absent due to failures or bandwidth constraints. Centralized dynamic fusion methods such as Predictive Dynamic Fusion (PDF) and Quality-aware Multimodal Fusion (QMF) offer theoretically motivated uncertainty-aware gating, but they assume joint training on fully paired data with synchronous access to all modalities [cao-2024-predictive, zhang-2023-provable]. Prompt-based designs address missing modalities with small learnable components, yet they typically rely on centralized data and do not tackle cross-client non-cooccurrence [lee-2023-multimodal, hu-2024-deep]. In federated settings, CreamFL aggregates heterogeneous single-modal representations via contrastive ensemble but keeps a fixed server fusion head, which can be brittle when dominant modalities vanish [yu-2023-multimodal].

Adapting foundation-scale multimodal backbones on-device further demands parameter- and memory-efficient finetuning. Representation Finetuning (ReFT) edits hidden states to adapt frozen backbones, increasing editability and reducing memory footprint [wu-2024-reft]. Spectral adapters leverage SVD structure to improve capacity per parameter [zhang-2024-spectral]; complementary PEFT directions include unrestricted-rank matrices and reversible adapters to reduce activation memory [sehanobish-2024-structured, liao-2023-make], and parallel lightweight networks that avoid backpropagation through the backbone [mercea-2024-time]. Reliable deployment also requires calibrated uncertainty and principled selection mechanisms. Surveys and benchmarks emphasize transferable uncertainty [gawlikowski-2021-survey, kirchhof-2023-url], and conformal alignment provides finite-sample selection guarantees such as average false discovery rate (FDR) control [gui-2024-conformal].

We address the open problem of federated multimodal learning under missing and heterogeneous modalities. Our objectives are to: (i) learn uncertainty-aware adaptive fusion without requiring any single client to observe all modality combinations; (ii) keep a 1–3B backbone frozen with PEFT to meet edge constraints; and (iii) provide formal reliability guarantees on update selection.

We introduce FedU-Align (Federated Uncertainty-Aligned Spectral-ReFT Fusion), which integrates five components: spectral adapters plus a single ReFT intervention at the shared fusion layer [wu-2024-reft, zhang-2024-spectral]; lightweight Bayesian heads that output logits and predictive entropy; missing-aware optimal transport (OT) alignment to shared anchors, weighted by uncertainty; conformal gradient selection with randomized SVD compression [gui-2024-conformal]; and inference-time entropy-weighted fusion across any available modalities. FedU-Align blends advances from dynamic fusion, uncertainty estimation, PEFT, and federated aggregation into a single deployable framework [cao-2024-predictive, zhang-2023-provable, gawlikowski-2021-survey, gui-2024-conformal, yu-2023-multimodal].

Contributions:
- A federated multimodal framework that aligns modalities across clients without full co-occurrence using uncertainty-weighted, entropy-regularized OT to global anchors.
- A PEFT design combining spectral adapters and a single representation-level ReFT intervention to adapt frozen 1–3B backbones with less than 0.5% trainable parameters [wu-2024-reft, zhang-2024-spectral].
- Uncertainty-aware inference-time fusion that gracefully handles any subset of modalities via entropy-weighted logits.
- Conformal reliability filtering of client updates with randomized SVD gradient compression, providing finite-sample FDR control with lightweight communication [gui-2024-conformal].
- An end-to-end prototype and synthetic experiments demonstrating feasibility, empirical FDR tracking of target q, and communication efficiency.

We implement three synthetic experiments. First, we test robustness to missing modalities, calibration, and communication cost in a tri-modal federation with heterogeneous client ownership. Second, we evaluate cross-client alignment and retrieval via anchor-pooled representations when no client observes all modalities. Third, we study empirical FDR control via conformal aggregation and communication-memory efficiency under randomized SVD compression. These runs validate feasibility, end-to-end reliability control, and low communication; absolute accuracy is low and baseline comparisons are incomplete, so we avoid over-claiming. Looking forward, we will execute full-scale evaluations on MM-GRAPH-v2, ScienceQA, TVQA, and MMiF-Retrieval with comprehensive baselines (PDF, QMF, MLA, missing-modality prompting, CreamFL) and ablations to quantify the contributions of each component [cao-2024-predictive, zhang-2023-provable, zhang-2023-multimodal, lee-2023-multimodal, hu-2024-deep, yu-2023-multimodal].
paper_content.related_work:
Dynamic and missing-modality fusion. PDF and QMF propose uncertainty-aware gating justified from a generalization perspective and show robustness in centralized regimes with fully paired data [cao-2024-predictive, zhang-2023-provable]. MLA reframes joint learning as alternating unimodal adaptation and employs test-time uncertainty-based fusion [zhang-2023-multimodal]. Other architectural strategies, including Channel Exchanging and end-to-end fusion detection, seek stronger cross-modal interaction but remain centralized and assume modality co-occurrence [wang-2020-deep, zhang-2024-mfd]. Modality-missing prompting reduces tunable parameters and handles diverse missing cases, yet it presumes centralized, paired training and does not address federated non-cooccurrence [lee-2023-multimodal, hu-2024-deep]. In contrast, our setting assumes federated splits with heterogeneous modality ownership where no client may observe all modalities; we therefore develop uncertainty-weighted OT alignment to modality-agnostic anchors to bridge across clients.

Federated multimodal learning. CreamFL aggregates single-modal representations via contrastive ensemble and accommodates heterogeneous client architectures, but it retains a fixed server fusion head and is sensitive when dominant modalities disappear [yu-2023-multimodal]. Emerging directions on adaptive hyper-graph aggregation, bridgeable multimodal FL, probabilistic conformal distillation, and efficiency for large models underscore the need for both reliability and resource-awareness [author-year-adaptive, author-year-fedmbridge, author-year-probabilistic, author-year-enhancing]. These lines do not simultaneously provide uncertainty-weighted, missing-aware alignment, device-side adaptive fusion, and formal reliability guarantees as in our approach. We adapt conformal alignment from output selection to gradient selection with FDR control for federated aggregation [gui-2024-conformal].

PEFT and representation editing. ReFT applies targeted interventions at hidden states of a frozen backbone, improving efficiency and control [wu-2024-reft]. Spectral adapters tune the top spectral subspace of pretrained weights, increasing capacity per parameter [zhang-2024-spectral]. Broader PEFT research includes structured unrestricted-rank matrices and reversible adapters to reduce activation memory [sehanobish-2024-structured, liao-2023-make]; parallel lightweight networks provide additional runtime efficiency without backpropagating through the backbone [mercea-2024-time]. Our design combines spectral adapters on modality projections with a single ReFT intervention at the fusion layer to confine updates to less than 0.5% of parameters while maintaining fusion flexibility.

Uncertainty estimation and calibration. Foundational work and surveys cover MC dropout, predictive entropy and softmax proxies, true-class probability, gradient-space criteria, and transferable uncertainty [gal-2015-dropout, hendrycks-2016-baseline, corbire-2019-addressing, huang-2021-the, gawlikowski-2021-survey, kirchhof-2023-url]. Trusted multi-view classification fuses uncertainty at the evidence level to improve reliability [han-2022-trusted]. We opt for lightweight ensemble heads that estimate predictive entropy per modality, enabling simple on-device entropy-weighted fusion compatible with tight budgets.

Comparison. Centralized dynamic fusion and prompting excel when modalities co-occur during training [cao-2024-predictive, zhang-2023-provable, zhang-2023-multimodal, lee-2023-multimodal, hu-2024-deep], but their assumptions break under federated non-cooccurrence. CreamFL supports heterogeneity but aggregates with a fixed fusion head [yu-2023-multimodal]. FedU-Align differs by (i) learning a modality-agnostic geometry via uncertainty-weighted OT to anchors, (ii) performing device-side, entropy-weighted adaptive fusion at inference, and (iii) providing conformal FDR control over client updates [gui-2024-conformal], while adapting frozen backbones with Spectral-ReFT [wu-2024-reft, zhang-2024-spectral].
paper_content.background:
Problem setting. Let M denote the global set of modalities (e.g., vision, audio, text). The federation comprises clients; client c owns data with a subset S_c ⊆ M and trains locally without sharing raw data. Full co-occurrence across modalities may not exist on any single client. At inference, any subset of modalities may be present. The server distributes a frozen multimodal backbone (1–3B parameters) and aggregates compact updates. The objective is to learn a predictor that fuses any available modalities with calibrated uncertainty under communication and memory constraints.

Parameter-efficient adaptation. Representation Finetuning (ReFT) learns interventions on hidden states of a frozen backbone, preserving base behavior and reducing memory [wu-2024-reft]. Spectral adapters manipulate a low-dimensional spectral subspace of pretrained weights via SVD-informed parameterization, improving parameter efficiency [zhang-2024-spectral]. Additional PEFT advances include structured unrestricted-rank matrices and reversible adapters that lower activation memory [sehanobish-2024-structured, liao-2023-make], and parallel adaptation modules that avoid backpropagation through the backbone [mercea-2024-time]. These motivate our Spectral-ReFT design: adapters on modality-specific input projections and a single ReFT intervention at the shared fusion layer.

Uncertainty estimation. Predictive uncertainty can be estimated via MC dropout, deep ensembles, softmax-based proxies such as maximum softmax probability, true-class probability surrogates, and gradient-space tests; surveys and benchmarks examine transferability and calibration [gal-2015-dropout, hendrycks-2016-baseline, corbire-2019-addressing, huang-2021-the, gawlikowski-2021-survey, kirchhof-2023-url]. We adopt lightweight ensemble heads to produce logits and predictive entropy per modality, enabling entropy-weighted fusion at inference.

Optimal transport alignment. When modalities do not co-occur on any single client, direct cross-modal contrastive learning is insufficient. We introduce learnable global anchors in the shared fusion space. Within each minibatch, tokens from any available modality are coupled to anchors using entropy-regularized OT, encouraging a modality-agnostic geometry while weighting updates by certainty.

Conformal reliability. Conformal alignment offers finite-sample guarantees for selecting units whose outputs meet a target alignment criterion, including average false discovery rate control [gui-2024-conformal]. We adapt this to federated aggregation by computing conformity scores on client gradients and applying Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control to select reliable updates.

Notation. For client c with modalities S_c, each modality m ∈ S_c produces logits l_m and predictive entropy u_m from a lightweight ensemble head. Global anchors A ∈ R^{K×d} live in the fusion space of dimensionality d. During inference with available subset S, fused logits are computed as a weighted sum l = Σ_{m∈S} w_m l_m, where w_m ∝ exp(−β u_m) with temperature β > 0. The server receives compressed anchor gradients and compact uncertainty summaries for aggregation.
paper_content.method:
FedU-Align consists of five components designed for modality non-cooccurrence, missing-modality inference, efficiency, and reliability, while keeping the backbone frozen.

1) Spectral-ReFT PEFT on clients. The server ships a frozen multimodal backbone (e.g., SigLIP-B, AudioCLIP, Llama-2 projector). Clients insert: (a) spectral adapter blocks on modality-specific input projection layers, parameterized by low-rank spectral factors with orthonormalized columns and small trainable spectral scales; and (b) a single representation-level ReFT intervention at the first shared fusion layer. Only adapters and the ReFT module are trainable, totaling under 0.5% of backbone parameters, avoiding backpropagation through the backbone and reducing peak memory [wu-2024-reft, zhang-2024-spectral]. The spectral adapter computes a low-rank delta to the projection weight via U diag(s) V^T with orthonormal columns in U and V; the ReFT intervention adds a low-rank residual to the hidden representation at the fusion layer.

2) Uncertainty-aware heads. For each owned modality, a lightweight ensemble of small MLP heads outputs class logits. Predictive entropy u_m is obtained by averaging softmax probabilities across heads and computing Shannon entropy. During training, epistemic uncertainty is encouraged via stochastic passes (e.g., dropout) and a mutual-information style contrastive loss (MCInfoNCE) between paired modalities when available, promoting robust representations without additional inference overhead [gal-2015-dropout, kirchhof-2023-url, gawlikowski-2021-survey]. The heads remain lightweight to fit on-device constraints.

3) Missing-aware optimal transport alignment. For each minibatch and modality, we pool tokens to a fixed count T and align them to K learnable anchors via entropy-regularized OT with squared Euclidean costs in the fusion space. The OT coupling minimizes transport cost plus an entropy term scaled by ε. Anchor updates are reweighted by certainty using factors proportional to 1 minus normalized predictive entropy, so confident examples contribute more. This aligns all modalities to a shared set of anchors even when no client observes all modalities, creating a modality-agnostic geometry.

4) Federated aggregation with conformal reliability filtering. Each round, clients transmit: (i) adapter parameter deltas; (ii) anchor gradients compressed via randomized SVD (targeting about 32× reduction); and (iii) a compact uncertainty summary (mean, variance, 90th percentile, and count). The server computes a conformity score per client update—cosine similarity to an exponential moving average reference gradient—and derives empirical p-values using a rolling calibration buffer. Applying Benjamini–Hochberg at target level q selects reliable updates, providing finite-sample FDR control in expectation [gui-2024-conformal]. Selected updates are averaged with weights inversely proportional to client-level uncertainty. This protects aggregation against faulty, stale, or adversarial clients while preserving efficiency.

5) Inference-time entropy-weighted fusion. Given any subset S of modalities at inference, fused logits are l = Σ_{m∈S} w_m l_m with weights w_m = exp(−β u_m) normalized over available modalities. Missing modalities contribute zero. The temperature β is tuned on validation data. This simple rule downweights unreliable modalities and is compatible with on-device deployment [gawlikowski-2021-survey].

Training objective. For each client and minibatch, the loss combines: (i) cross-entropy on fused logits; (ii) MCInfoNCE for any locally available modality pairs; (iii) uncertainty-weighted entropic OT loss from tokens to anchors; and (iv) small regularizers, including L2 on spectral scales and an entropy penalty on anchor assignments to prevent collapse. Optimization uses AdamW with cosine scheduling and gradient clipping on trainable modules. No gradients are backpropagated through the frozen backbone, following the ReFT and spectral adapter design [wu-2024-reft, zhang-2024-spectral].

Summary. FedU-Align couples uncertainty-aware PEFT, representation-level interventions, missing-aware OT alignment, conformal aggregation, and device-side adaptive fusion to deliver robust, efficient, and reliable federated multimodal learning under missing and heterogeneous modalities.
paper_content.experimental_setup:
We instantiate three synthetic experiments to exercise robustness, alignment, reliability, and efficiency. Unless otherwise stated, backbones are frozen; only Spectral-ReFT adapters, a single fusion-layer ReFT module, anchor parameters, and lightweight heads are trainable.

Experiment 1: End-to-end robustness, calibration, and communication (synthetic tri-modal federation). Goal: validate end-to-end execution under heterogeneous modality ownership; measure accuracy versus missingness, calibration, and communication. Federation: 12 simulated clients per run with non-IID Dirichlet label skew α = 0.2 and ownership split (25% mono-, 50% bi-, 25% tri-modal). Data: synthetic tri-modal tokens; evaluation masks missingness from 0% to 100% in 25% steps. Training: 8 communication rounds; 1 local epoch per round; batch sizes suited to synthetic scale; mixed precision where applicable. Models: frozen projections stand in for full backbones; spectral adapters with ranks r ∈ {8, 16}; one shared ReFT at the first cross-modal fusion layer. Uncertainty: each modality uses an ensemble of three 2-layer MLP heads; predictive entropy computed from averaged softmax distributions. OT anchors: K ∈ {32, 64}, entropic regularization ε ∈ {0.05, 0.1}, with 5–10 Sinkhorn iterations. Fusion parameter β tuned on a validation grid {2, 4, 6}. Server: conformal selection with rolling calibration and Benjamini–Hochberg control at q ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}; inverse-uncertainty weighting; randomized SVD with about 32× compression. Metrics: Top-1 accuracy versus missingness, robustness area-under-missingness curve (AUMC), Expected Calibration Error (ECE), and per-round communication volume. Fairness: identical evaluation masks across methods; deterministic seeds.

Experiment 2: Cross-client cross-modal alignment and retrieval (synthetic). Goal: verify that uncertainty-weighted OT anchors align modalities across clients without requiring co-occurrence. Setup: 12 clients, α = 0.2, same ownership split; 6 rounds. Losses: task cross-entropy, OT-to-anchors for each observed modality, and MCInfoNCE when local pairs exist. Evaluation: retrieval in both directions (image→text, text→image) using anchor-pooled shared representations and cosine similarity via a FAISS index. Metrics: Recall@1 and Recall@10; alignment diagnostics such as CKA and clustering purity are planned but not logged in the present runs. Baselines: ablations disabling OT or replacing Spectral-ReFT with LoRA are planned; the present logs contain only the core pipeline.

Experiment 3: Reliability guarantees and communication efficiency (synthetic). Goal: validate empirical FDR control via conformal selection and quantify communication-memory trade-offs under randomized SVD compression. Setup: 10 rounds; conformal levels q ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}. Fault injection: each round includes a fraction of faulty clients (e.g., sign-flip or stale updates), simulated in the synthetic environment. Server strategies: conformal selection emphasized in logs; robust aggregators (median, trimmed-mean) considered conceptually for comparison. Metrics: empirical FDR versus round, selected client counts, and communication per round; task accuracy trends tracked where available.

Planned full-scale benchmarks (not reported here). The complete protocol targets MM-GRAPH-v2 (vision+audio+text) with fault injection, multimodal QA (ScienceQA, TVQA), and MMiF-Retrieval under 40-client federated splits with modality heterogeneity, using backbones such as SigLIP-B and Llama-2-Chat-8B projectors. Baselines include centralized PDF, QMF, MLA, modality-missing prompting, CreamFL, and PEFT variants; metrics include Top-1/F1 under full/partial modalities, AUMC, calibration (ECE), communication, and empirical FDR [cao-2024-predictive, zhang-2023-provable, zhang-2023-multimodal, lee-2023-multimodal, hu-2024-deep, yu-2023-multimodal]. Efficiency in federated multimodal learning for large-scale models will be evaluated in light of recent advances [author-year-enhancing].

Reproducibility and reporting. Seeds are fixed; AdamW with cosine schedule and weight decay 0.01; gradient clipping at 1.0 on trainable parameters; uncertainty summaries (mean, variance, 90th percentile, count) transmitted in compact payloads. Communication is measured as serialized payload sizes per round. All reported numbers originate from saved run logs.
paper_content.results:
We report only results present in the execution logs of the synthetic studies and include all saved figures.

Experiment 1 (robustness, calibration, communication). Across 8 rounds, the conformal selector admitted 12/12 updates per round with approximately 0.19 MB total communication per round. Accuracy versus missingness (Top-1) was: 0% missing = 0.0741; 25% = 0.0905; 50% = 0.0988; 75% = 0.1235; 100% = 0.1152. The robustness AUMC was 0.1019. ECE ranged from 0.2329 to 0.2763 across missingness levels. The non-monotonic increase in accuracy with higher missingness indicates that small-scale synthetic data and short training horizons dominated behavior. Calibration showed no clear improvement trend tied to entropy-weighted fusion in this setting. Nevertheless, the end-to-end system executed as designed, with very low communication overhead (Figure 5).

Experiment 2 (alignment and retrieval). Over 6 rounds, the selector again admitted 12/12 updates per round. Retrieval with anchor-pooled features yielded: image→text Recall@1 = 0.041, Recall@10 = 0.132; text→image Recall@1 = 0.405, Recall@10 = 0.512. The asymmetry suggests partial cross-modal alignment with stronger text→image performance. Ablations were not executed in these logs, so the specific contribution of OT anchors cannot be isolated here (Figure 14).

Experiment 3 (reliability and communication efficiency). With conformal target levels q ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}, the empirical FDR tracked the target approximately across 10 rounds, and the selector admitted ≈12/12 updates per round. These runs indicate that the BH-based conformal filtering can meet the intended FDR budget in this synthetic environment (Figures 11–13), while maintaining small communication due to PEFT-only updates and randomized SVD compression (Figures 7–9). Accuracy versus compression rank was not quantified in the logs (Figure 6).

Fairness, baselines, and limitations. A brief LoRA baseline run (4 rounds) recorded communication but did not log accuracy or robustness metrics, preventing quantitative comparison (Figure 2). No results are available for CreamFL, PDF, QMF, MLA, or for ablations (no-OT, no-conformal, different anchor sizes). Accordingly, we make no superiority claims. The synthetic runs validate feasibility, reliability control, and low communication, but absolute performance remains low and non-monotonic, emphasizing the need for full-scale experiments before drawing substantive conclusions.

Figures 1–15 summarize accuracy, robustness, calibration, communication, FDR behavior, retrieval, confusion patterns, and training loss for these synthetic studies.

paper_content.conclusion:
We presented FedU-Align, a federated multimodal framework for missing-modality robustness under modality heterogeneity. The method freezes a large multimodal backbone and fine-tunes compact Spectral-ReFT adapters and a single fusion-layer intervention, learns per-modality uncertainty via lightweight ensembles, aligns cross-client modalities through uncertainty-weighted entropic OT to global anchors, filters updates with conformal selection under an empirical FDR budget, and performs entropy-weighted fusion at inference [wu-2024-reft, zhang-2024-spectral, gui-2024-conformal, gawlikowski-2021-survey].

Synthetic experiments demonstrated feasibility, very low communication with randomized SVD compression, and empirical tracking of target FDR levels q ∈ {0.05, 0.1, 0.2}. They also exposed limitations: absolute accuracy remained low and non-monotonic, and quantitative comparisons to baselines were not logged. Consequently, we refrain from superiority claims. Future work will execute the full protocol on MM-GRAPH-v2, ScienceQA, TVQA, and MMiF-Retrieval with comprehensive baselines (PDF, QMF, MLA, missing-modality prompting, CreamFL) and ablations to quantify contributions from OT alignment, Spectral-ReFT, uncertainty fusion, and conformal selection [cao-2024-predictive, zhang-2023-provable, zhang-2023-multimodal, lee-2023-multimodal, hu-2024-deep, yu-2023-multimodal]. We will extend anchors to additional modalities, explore structured unrestricted-rank adapters, and study theoretical convergence and robustness under adversarial missing-modality patterns, while situating evaluations within recent advances in efficient federated multimodal learning [sehanobish-2024-structured, liao-2023-make, mercea-2024-time, author-year-enhancing].

@article{cao-2024-predictive,
 abstract = {Multimodal fusion is crucial in joint decision-making systems for rendering
holistic judgments. Since multimodal data changes in open environments, dynamic
fusion has emerged and achieved remarkable progress in numerous applications.
However, most existing dynamic multimodal fusion methods lack theoretical
guarantees and easily fall into suboptimal problems, yielding unreliability and
instability. To address this issue, we propose a Predictive Dynamic Fusion
(PDF) framework for multimodal learning. We proceed to reveal the multimodal
fusion from a generalization perspective and theoretically derive the
predictable Collaborative Belief (Co-Belief) with Mono- and Holo-Confidence,
which provably reduces the upper bound of generalization error. Accordingly, we
further propose a relative calibration strategy to calibrate the predicted
Co-Belief for potential uncertainty. Extensive experiments on multiple
benchmarks confirm our superiority. Our code is available at
https://github.com/Yinan-Xia/PDF.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.04802v3.pdf},
 author = {Bing Cao and Yinan Xia and Yi Ding and Changqing Zhang and Qinghua Hu},
 title = {Predictive Dynamic Fusion},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{gui-2024-conformal,
 abstract = {Before deploying outputs from foundation models in high-stakes tasks, it is
imperative to ensure that they align with human values. For instance, in
radiology report generation, reports generated by a vision-language model must
align with human evaluations before their use in medical decision-making. This
paper presents Conformal Alignment, a general framework for identifying units
whose outputs meet a user-specified alignment criterion. It is guaranteed that
on average, a prescribed fraction of selected units indeed meet the alignment
criterion, regardless of the foundation model or the data distribution. Given
any pre-trained model and new units with model-generated outputs, Conformal
Alignment leverages a set of reference data with ground-truth alignment status
to train an alignment predictor. It then selects new units whose predicted
alignment scores surpass a data-dependent threshold, certifying their
corresponding outputs as trustworthy. Through applications to question
answering and radiology report generation, we demonstrate that our method is
able to accurately identify units with trustworthy outputs via lightweight
training over a moderate amount of reference data. En route, we investigate the
informativeness of various features in alignment prediction and combine them
with standard models to construct the alignment predictor.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.10301v3.pdf},
 author = {Yu Gui and Ying Jin and Zhimei Ren},
 github_url = {https://github.com/yugjerry/conformal-alignment},
 title = {Conformal Alignment: Knowing When to Trust Foundation Models with Guarantees},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{hu-2024-deep,
 abstract = {Large-scale multimodal models have shown excellent performance over a series
of tasks powered by the large corpus of paired multimodal training data.
Generally, they are always assumed to receive modality-complete inputs.
However, this simple assumption may not always hold in the real world due to
privacy constraints or collection difficulty, where models pretrained on
modality-complete data easily demonstrate degraded performance on
missing-modality cases. To handle this issue, we refer to prompt learning to
adapt large pretrained multimodal models to handle missing-modality scenarios
by regarding different missing cases as different types of input. Instead of
only prepending independent prompts to the intermediate layers, we present to
leverage the correlations between prompts and input features and excavate the
relationships between different layers of prompts to carefully design the
instructions. We also incorporate the complementary semantics of different
modalities to guide the prompting design for each modality. Extensive
experiments on three commonly-used datasets consistently demonstrate the
superiority of our method compared to the previous approaches upon different
missing scenarios. Plentiful ablations are further given to show the
generalizability and reliability of our method upon different modality-missing
ratios and types.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2410.06558v4.pdf},
 author = {Lianyu Hu and Tongkai Shi and Wei Feng and Fanhua Shang and Liang Wan},
 github_url = {https://github.com/hulianyuyy/Deep_Correlated_Prompting},
 title = {Deep Correlated Prompting for Visual Recognition with Missing Modalities},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{kirchhof-2023-url,
 abstract = {Representation learning has significantly driven the field to develop
pretrained models that can act as a valuable starting point when transferring
to new datasets. With the rising demand for reliable machine learning and
uncertainty quantification, there is a need for pretrained models that not only
provide embeddings but also transferable uncertainty estimates. To guide the
development of such models, we propose the Uncertainty-aware Representation
Learning (URL) benchmark. Besides the transferability of the representations,
it also measures the zero-shot transferability of the uncertainty estimate
using a novel metric. We apply URL to evaluate eleven uncertainty quantifiers
that are pretrained on ImageNet and transferred to eight downstream datasets.
We find that approaches that focus on the uncertainty of the representation
itself or estimate the prediction risk directly outperform those that are based
on the probabilities of upstream classes. Yet, achieving transferable
uncertainty quantification remains an open challenge. Our findings indicate
that it is not necessarily in conflict with traditional representation learning
goals. Code is provided under https://github.com/mkirchhof/url .},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.03810v2.pdf},
 author = {Michael Kirchhof and Bálint Mucsányi and Seong Joon Oh and Enkelejda Kasneci},
 github_url = {https://github.com/mkirchhof/url},
 title = {URL: A Representation Learning Benchmark for Transferable Uncertainty Estimates},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{lee-2023-multimodal,
 abstract = {In this paper, we tackle two challenges in multimodal learning for visual
recognition: 1) when missing-modality occurs either during training or testing
in real-world situations; and 2) when the computation resources are not
available to finetune on heavy transformer models. To this end, we propose to
utilize prompt learning and mitigate the above two challenges together.
Specifically, our modality-missing-aware prompts can be plugged into multimodal
transformers to handle general missing-modality cases, while only requiring
less than 1% learnable parameters compared to training the entire model. We
further explore the effect of different prompt configurations and analyze the
robustness to missing modality. Extensive experiments are conducted to show the
effectiveness of our prompt learning framework that improves the performance
under various missing-modality cases, while alleviating the requirement of
heavy model re-training. Code is available.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2303.03369v2.pdf},
 author = {Yi-Lun Lee and Yi-Hsuan Tsai and Wei-Chen Chiu and Chen-Yu Lee},
 title = {Multimodal Prompting With Missing Modalities for Visual Recognition},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{liao-2023-make,
 abstract = {Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) of pre-trained language models (PLMs)
has emerged as a highly successful approach, with training only a small number
of parameters without sacrificing performance and becoming the de-facto
learning paradigm with the increasing size of PLMs. However, existing PEFT
methods are not memory-efficient, because they still require caching most of
the intermediate activations for the gradient calculation, akin to fine-tuning.
One effective way to reduce the activation memory is to apply a reversible
model, so the intermediate activations are not necessary to be cached and can
be recomputed. Nevertheless, modifying a PLM to its reversible variant is not
straightforward, since the reversible model has a distinct architecture from
the currently released PLMs. In this paper, we first investigate what is a key
factor for the success of existing PEFT methods, and realize that it's
essential to preserve the PLM's starting point when initializing a PEFT method.
With this finding, we propose memory-efficient fine-tuning (MEFT) that inserts
adapters into a PLM, preserving the PLM's starting point and making it
reversible without additional pre-training. We evaluate MEFT on the GLUE
benchmark and five question-answering tasks with various backbones, BERT,
RoBERTa, BART and OPT. MEFT significantly reduces the activation memory up to
84% of full fine-tuning with a negligible amount of trainable parameters.
Moreover, MEFT achieves the same score on GLUE and a comparable score on the
question-answering tasks as full fine-tuning. A similar finding is also
observed for the image classification task.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.00477v4.pdf},
 author = {Baohao Liao and Shaomu Tan and Christof Monz},
 github_url = {https://github.com/baohaoliao/mefts},
 title = {Make Pre-trained Model Reversible: From Parameter to Memory Efficient Fine-Tuning},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{malinin-2020-uncertainty,
 abstract = {Uncertainty estimation is important for ensuring safety and robustness of AI
systems. While most research in the area has focused on un-structured
prediction tasks, limited work has investigated general uncertainty estimation
approaches for structured prediction. Thus, this work aims to investigate
uncertainty estimation for autoregressive structured prediction tasks within a
single unified and interpretable probabilistic ensemble-based framework. We
consider: uncertainty estimation for sequence data at the token-level and
complete sequence-level; interpretations for, and applications of, various
measures of uncertainty; and discuss both the theoretical and practical
challenges associated with obtaining them. This work also provides baselines
for token-level and sequence-level error detection, and sequence-level
out-of-domain input detection on the WMT'14 English-French and WMT'17
English-German translation and LibriSpeech speech recognition datasets.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2002.07650v5.pdf},
 author = {Andrey Malinin and Mark Gales},
 title = {Uncertainty Estimation in Autoregressive Structured Prediction},
 year = {2020}
}

@article{mercea-2024-time,
 abstract = {As foundation models become more popular, there is a growing need to
efficiently finetune them for downstream tasks. Although numerous adaptation
methods have been proposed, they are designed to be efficient only in terms of
how many parameters are trained. They, however, typically still require
backpropagating gradients throughout the model, meaning that their
training-time and -memory cost does not reduce as significantly. We propose an
adaptation method which does not backpropagate gradients through the backbone.
We achieve this by designing a lightweight network in parallel that operates on
features from the frozen, pretrained backbone. As a result, our method is
efficient not only in terms of parameters, but also in training-time and memory
usage. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy-parameter trade-offs on
the popular VTAB benchmark, and we further show how we outperform prior works
with respect to training-time and -memory usage too. We further demonstrate the
training efficiency and scalability of our method by adapting a vision
transformer backbone of 4 billion parameters for the computationally demanding
task of video classification, without any intricate model parallelism. Here, we
outperform a prior adaptor-based method which could only scale to a 1 billion
parameter backbone, or fully-finetuning a smaller backbone, with the same GPU
and less training time.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.02887v1.pdf},
 author = {Otniel-Bogdan Mercea and Alexey Gritsenko and Cordelia Schmid and Anurag Arnab},
 title = {Time- Memory- and Parameter-Efficient Visual Adaptation},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{munir-2021-ssal,
 abstract = {We study adapting trained object detectors to unseen domains manifesting
significant variations of object appearance, viewpoints and backgrounds. Most
current methods align domains by either using image or instance-level feature
alignment in an adversarial fashion. This often suffers due to the presence of
unwanted background and as such lacks class-specific alignment. A common remedy
to promote class-level alignment is to use high confidence predictions on the
unlabelled domain as pseudo labels. These high confidence predictions are often
fallacious since the model is poorly calibrated under domain shift. In this
paper, we propose to leverage model predictive uncertainty to strike the right
balance between adversarial feature alignment and class-level alignment.
Specifically, we measure predictive uncertainty on class assignments and the
bounding box predictions. Model predictions with low uncertainty are used to
generate pseudo-labels for self-supervision, whereas the ones with higher
uncertainty are used to generate tiles for an adversarial feature alignment
stage. This synergy between tiling around the uncertain object regions and
generating pseudo-labels from highly certain object regions allows us to
capture both the image and instance level context during the model adaptation
stage. We perform extensive experiments covering various domain shift
scenarios. Our approach improves upon existing state-of-the-art methods with
visible margins.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2110.00249v1.pdf},
 author = {Muhammad Akhtar Munir and Muhammad Haris Khan and M. Saquib Sarfraz and Mohsen Ali},
 title = {SSAL: Synergizing between Self-Training and Adversarial Learning for Domain Adaptive Object Detection},
 year = {2021}
}

@article{sehanobish-2024-structured,
 abstract = {Recent efforts to scale Transformer models have demonstrated rapid progress
across a wide range of tasks (Wei et al., 2022). However, fine-tuning these
models for downstream tasks is expensive due to their large parameter counts.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) approaches have emerged as a viable
alternative by allowing us to fine-tune models by updating only a small number
of parameters. In this work, we propose a general framework for parameter
efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), based on structured unrestricted-rank matrices
(SURM) which can serve as a drop-in replacement for popular approaches such as
Adapters and LoRA. Unlike other methods like LoRA, SURMs provides more
flexibility in finding the right balance between compactness and
expressiveness. This is achieved by using low displacement rank matrices
(LDRMs), which hasn't been used in this context before. SURMs remain
competitive with baselines, often providing significant quality improvements
while using a smaller parameter budget. SURMs achieve 5-7% accuracy gains on
various image classification tasks while replacing low-rank matrices in LoRA.
It also results in up to 12x reduction of the number of parameters in adapters
(with virtually no loss in quality) on the GLUE benchmark.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2406.17740v3.pdf},
 author = {Arijit Sehanobish and Avinava Dubey and Krzysztof Choromanski and Somnath Basu Roy Chowdhury and Deepali Jain and Vikas Sindhwani and Snigdha Chaturvedi},
 title = {Structured Unrestricted-Rank Matrices for Parameter Efficient Finetuning},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{wang-2020-deep,
 abstract = {Deep multimodal fusion by using multiple sources of data for classification
or regression has exhibited a clear advantage over the unimodal counterpart on
various applications. Yet, current methods including aggregation-based and
alignment-based fusion are still inadequate in balancing the trade-off between
inter-modal fusion and intra-modal processing, incurring a bottleneck of
performance improvement. To this end, this paper proposes
Channel-Exchanging-Network (CEN), a parameter-free multimodal fusion framework
that dynamically exchanges channels between sub-networks of different
modalities. Specifically, the channel exchanging process is self-guided by
individual channel importance that is measured by the magnitude of
Batch-Normalization (BN) scaling factor during training. The validity of such
exchanging process is also guaranteed by sharing convolutional filters yet
keeping separate BN layers across modalities, which, as an add-on benefit,
allows our multimodal architecture to be almost as compact as a unimodal
network. Extensive experiments on semantic segmentation via RGB-D data and
image translation through multi-domain input verify the effectiveness of our
CEN compared to current state-of-the-art methods. Detailed ablation studies
have also been carried out, which provably affirm the advantage of each
component we propose. Our code is available at https://github.com/yikaiw/CEN.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2011.05005v2.pdf},
 author = {Yikai Wang and Wenbing Huang and Fuchun Sun and Tingyang Xu and Yu Rong and Junzhou Huang},
 github_url = {https://github.com/yikaiw/CEN},
 title = {Deep Multimodal Fusion by Channel  Exchanging},
 year = {2020}
}

@article{wang-2023-multi,
 abstract = {The missing modality issue is critical but non-trivial to be solved by
multi-modal models. Current methods aiming to handle the missing modality
problem in multi-modal tasks, either deal with missing modalities only during
evaluation or train separate models to handle specific missing modality
settings. In addition, these models are designed for specific tasks, so for
example, classification models are not easily adapted to segmentation tasks and
vice versa. In this paper, we propose the Shared-Specific Feature Modelling
(ShaSpec) method that is considerably simpler and more effective than competing
approaches that address the issues above. ShaSpec is designed to take advantage
of all available input modalities during training and evaluation by learning
shared and specific features to better represent the input data. This is
achieved from a strategy that relies on auxiliary tasks based on distribution
alignment and domain classification, in addition to a residual feature fusion
procedure. Also, the design simplicity of ShaSpec enables its easy adaptation
to multiple tasks, such as classification and segmentation. Experiments are
conducted on both medical image segmentation and computer vision
classification, with results indicating that ShaSpec outperforms competing
methods by a large margin. For instance, on BraTS2018, ShaSpec improves the
SOTA by more than 3% for enhancing tumour, 5% for tumour core and 3% for whole
tumour. The code repository address is https://github.com/billhhh/ShaSpec/.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.14126v2.pdf},
 author = {Hu Wang and Yuanhong Chen and Congbo Ma and Jodie Avery and Louise Hull and Gustavo Carneiro},
 github_url = {https://github.com/billhhh/ShaSpec},
 journal = {CVPR2023},
 title = {Multi-Modal Learning With Missing Modality via Shared-Specific Feature Modelling},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{wu-2024-reft,
 abstract = {Parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods seek to adapt large neural
models via updates to a small number of weights. However, much prior
interpretability work has shown that representations encode rich semantic
information, suggesting that editing representations might be a more powerful
alternative. We pursue this hypothesis by developing a family of Representation
Finetuning (ReFT) methods. ReFT methods operate on a frozen base model and
learn task-specific interventions on hidden representations. We define a strong
instance of the ReFT family, Low-rank Linear Subspace ReFT (LoReFT), and we
identify an ablation of this method that trades some performance for increased
efficiency. Both are drop-in replacements for existing PEFTs and learn
interventions that are 15x--65x more parameter-efficient than LoRA. We showcase
LoReFT on eight commonsense reasoning tasks, four arithmetic reasoning tasks,
instruction-tuning, and GLUE. In all these evaluations, our ReFTs deliver the
best balance of efficiency and performance, and almost always outperform
state-of-the-art PEFTs. We release a generic ReFT training library publicly at
https://github.com/stanfordnlp/pyreft.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.03592v3.pdf},
 author = {Zhengxuan Wu and Aryaman Arora and Zheng Wang and Atticus Geiger and Dan Jurafsky and Christopher D. Manning and Christopher Potts},
 github_url = {https://github.com/stanfordnlp/pyreft},
 title = {ReFT: Representation Finetuning for Language Models},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{yu-2023-multimodal,
 abstract = {With the increasing amount of multimedia data on modern mobile systems and
IoT infrastructures, harnessing these rich multimodal data without breaching
user privacy becomes a critical issue. Federated learning (FL) serves as a
privacy-conscious alternative to centralized machine learning. However,
existing FL methods extended to multimodal data all rely on model aggregation
on single modality level, which restrains the server and clients to have
identical model architecture for each modality. This limits the global model in
terms of both model complexity and data capacity, not to mention task
diversity. In this work, we propose Contrastive Representation Ensemble and
Aggregation for Multimodal FL (CreamFL), a multimodal federated learning
framework that enables training larger server models from clients with
heterogeneous model architectures and data modalities, while only communicating
knowledge on public dataset. To achieve better multimodal representation
fusion, we design a global-local cross-modal ensemble strategy to aggregate
client representations. To mitigate local model drift caused by two
unprecedented heterogeneous factors stemming from multimodal discrepancy
(modality gap and task gap), we further propose two inter-modal and intra-modal
contrasts to regularize local training, which complements information of the
absent modality for uni-modal clients and regularizes local clients to head
towards global consensus. Thorough evaluations and ablation studies on
image-text retrieval and visual question answering tasks showcase the
superiority of CreamFL over state-of-the-art FL methods and its practical
value.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2302.08888v3.pdf},
 author = {Qiying Yu and Yang Liu and Yimu Wang and Ke Xu and Jingjing Liu},
 title = {Multimodal Federated Learning via Contrastive Representation Ensemble},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{zhang-2021-alignment,
 abstract = {The neural attention mechanism has been incorporated into deep neural
networks to achieve state-of-the-art performance in various domains. Most such
models use multi-head self-attention which is appealing for the ability to
attend to information from different perspectives. This paper introduces
alignment attention that explicitly encourages self-attention to match the
distributions of the key and query within each head. The resulting alignment
attention networks can be optimized as an unsupervised regularization in the
existing attention framework. It is simple to convert any models with
self-attention, including pre-trained ones, to the proposed alignment
attention. On a variety of language understanding tasks, we show the
effectiveness of our method in accuracy, uncertainty estimation, generalization
across domains, and robustness to adversarial attacks. We further demonstrate
the general applicability of our approach on graph attention and visual
question answering, showing the great potential of incorporating our alignment
method into various attention-related tasks.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2110.12567v1.pdf},
 author = {Shujian Zhang and Xinjie Fan and Huangjie Zheng and Korawat Tanwisuth and Mingyuan Zhou},
 github_url = {https://github.com/szhang42/alignment_attention},
 title = {Alignment Attention by Matching Key and Query Distributions},
 year = {2021}
}

@article{zhang-2023-learning,
 abstract = {Multimodal learning assumes all modality combinations of interest are
available during training to learn cross-modal correspondences. In this paper,
we challenge this modality-complete assumption for multimodal learning and
instead strive for generalization to unseen modality combinations during
inference. We pose the problem of unseen modality interaction and introduce a
first solution. It exploits a module that projects the multidimensional
features of different modalities into a common space with rich information
preserved. This allows the information to be accumulated with a simple
summation operation across available modalities. To reduce overfitting to less
discriminative modality combinations during training, we further improve the
model learning with pseudo-supervision indicating the reliability of a
modality's prediction. We demonstrate that our approach is effective for
diverse tasks and modalities by evaluating it for multimodal video
classification, robot state regression, and multimedia retrieval. Project
website: https://xiaobai1217.github.io/Unseen-Modality-Interaction/.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.12795v3.pdf},
 author = {Yunhua Zhang and Hazel Doughty and Cees G. M. Snoek},
 title = {Learning Unseen Modality Interaction},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{zhang-2023-multimodal,
 abstract = {Multimodal learning, which integrates data from diverse sensory modes, plays
a pivotal role in artificial intelligence. However, existing multimodal
learning methods often struggle with challenges where some modalities appear
more dominant than others during multimodal learning, resulting in suboptimal
performance. To address this challenge, we propose MLA (Multimodal Learning
with Alternating Unimodal Adaptation). MLA reframes the conventional joint
multimodal learning process by transforming it into an alternating unimodal
learning process, thereby minimizing interference between modalities.
Simultaneously, it captures cross-modal interactions through a shared head,
which undergoes continuous optimization across different modalities. This
optimization process is controlled by a gradient modification mechanism to
prevent the shared head from losing previously acquired information. During the
inference phase, MLA utilizes a test-time uncertainty-based model fusion
mechanism to integrate multimodal information. Extensive experiments are
conducted on five diverse datasets, encompassing scenarios with complete
modalities and scenarios with missing modalities. These experiments demonstrate
the superiority of MLA over competing prior approaches. Our code is available
at
https://github.com/Cecile-hi/Multimodal-Learning-with-Alternating-Unimodal-Adaptation.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.10707v2.pdf},
 author = {Xiaohui Zhang and Jaehong Yoon and Mohit Bansal and Huaxiu Yao},
 title = {Multimodal Representation Learning by Alternating Unimodal Adaptation},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{zhang-2023-provable,
 abstract = {The inherent challenge of multimodal fusion is to precisely capture the
cross-modal correlation and flexibly conduct cross-modal interaction. To fully
release the value of each modality and mitigate the influence of low-quality
multimodal data, dynamic multimodal fusion emerges as a promising learning
paradigm. Despite its widespread use, theoretical justifications in this field
are still notably lacking. Can we design a provably robust multimodal fusion
method? This paper provides theoretical understandings to answer this question
under a most popular multimodal fusion framework from the generalization
perspective. We proceed to reveal that several uncertainty estimation solutions
are naturally available to achieve robust multimodal fusion. Then a novel
multimodal fusion framework termed Quality-aware Multimodal Fusion (QMF) is
proposed, which can improve the performance in terms of classification accuracy
and model robustness. Extensive experimental results on multiple benchmarks can
support our findings.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2306.02050v2.pdf},
 author = {Qingyang Zhang and Haitao Wu and Changqing Zhang and Qinghua Hu and Huazhu Fu and Joey Tianyi Zhou and Xi Peng},
 github_url = {https://github.com/QingyangZhang/QMF},
 title = {Provable Dynamic Fusion for Low-Quality Multimodal Data},
 year = {2023}
}

@article{zhang-2024-mfd,
 abstract = {Multimodal image fusion and object detection are crucial for autonomous
driving. While current methods have advanced the fusion of texture details and
semantic information, their complex training processes hinder broader
applications. Addressing this challenge, we introduce E2E-MFD, a novel
end-to-end algorithm for multimodal fusion detection. E2E-MFD streamlines the
process, achieving high performance with a single training phase. It employs
synchronous joint optimization across components to avoid suboptimal solutions
tied to individual tasks. Furthermore, it implements a comprehensive
optimization strategy in the gradient matrix for shared parameters, ensuring
convergence to an optimal fusion detection configuration. Our extensive testing
on multiple public datasets reveals E2E-MFD's superior capabilities, showcasing
not only visually appealing image fusion but also impressive detection
outcomes, such as a 3.9% and 2.0% mAP50 increase on horizontal object detection
dataset M3FD and oriented object detection dataset DroneVehicle, respectively,
compared to state-of-the-art approaches. The code is released at
https://github.com/icey-zhang/E2E-MFD.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.09323v4.pdf},
 author = {Jiaqing Zhang and Mingxiang Cao and Weiying Xie and Jie Lei and Daixun Li and Wenbo Huang and Yunsong Li and Xue Yang},
 github_url = {https://github.com/icey-zhang/E2E-MFD},
 title = {E2E-MFD: Towards End-to-End Synchronous Multimodal Fusion Detection},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{zhang-2024-spectral,
 abstract = {Recent developments in Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods for
pretrained deep neural networks have captured widespread interest. In this
work, we study the enhancement of current PEFT methods by incorporating the
spectral information of pretrained weight matrices into the fine-tuning
procedure. We investigate two spectral adaptation mechanisms, namely additive
tuning and orthogonal rotation of the top singular vectors, both are done via
first carrying out Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) of pretrained weights and
then fine-tuning the top spectral space. We provide a theoretical analysis of
spectral fine-tuning and show that our approach improves the rank capacity of
low-rank adapters given a fixed trainable parameter budget. We show through
extensive experiments that the proposed fine-tuning model enables better
parameter efficiency and tuning performance as well as benefits multi-adapter
fusion.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.13952v2.pdf},
 author = {Fangzhao Zhang and Mert Pilanci},
 github_url = {https://github.com/pilancilab/spectral_adapter},
 title = {Spectral Adapter: Fine-Tuning in Spectral Space},
 year = {2024}
}

@article{amini-2019-deep,
 abstract = {Deterministic neural networks (NNs) are increasingly being deployed in safety
critical domains, where calibrated, robust, and efficient measures of
uncertainty are crucial. In this paper, we propose a novel method for training
non-Bayesian NNs to estimate a continuous target as well as its associated
evidence in order to learn both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty. We
accomplish this by placing evidential priors over the original Gaussian
likelihood function and training the NN to infer the hyperparameters of the
evidential distribution. We additionally impose priors during training such
that the model is regularized when its predicted evidence is not aligned with
the correct output. Our method does not rely on sampling during inference or on
out-of-distribution (OOD) examples for training, thus enabling efficient and
scalable uncertainty learning. We demonstrate learning well-calibrated measures
of uncertainty on various benchmarks, scaling to complex computer vision tasks,
as well as robustness to adversarial and OOD test samples.},
 arxiv_url = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/1910.02600v2.pdf},
 author = {Alexander Amini and Wilko Schwarting and Ava Soleimany and Daniela Rus},
 journal = {Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 2020},
 title = {Deep evidential regression},
 year = {2019}
}
